c.tagline: Scotland's warm-hearted second city — Victorian grandeur, music, and legendary nightlife.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed black hackney cabs are metered and can be hailed on the street; private-hire cars (including Uber and Bolt) must be pre-booked through the app.

emergency.note: 112 also works and connects to police, fire, and ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Very safe centrally; caution in some East End areas at night

hood_desc: The commercial and cultural core around George Square, Buchanan Street and the 'Style Mile' of shops, with grand Victorian buildings, theatres and the two main rail stations; best for first-timers who want everything on the doorstep.
A stylish grid of converted 18th-century warehouses just east of the centre, packed with bars, restaurants, boutiques and the Gallery of Modern Art; lively day and night and popular for going out.

Glasgow's leafy, bohemian quarter around Byres Road and cobbled Ashton Lane, home to the University of Glasgow, Kelvingrove Art Gallery and the Botanic Gardens; full of cafes, bookshops and student energy.
A former industrial strip by the Clyde reborn as the city's hippest food-and-drink destination, with acclaimed restaurants and cocktail bars along Argyle Street next to the SEC and OVO Hydro.
A relaxed, residential swathe south of the river taking in Shawlands, Queen's Park and Pollok Country Park (with the Burrell Collection); quieter and more local, good for a calmer base.
lodging: Hotel du Vin at One Devonshire Gardens

water.note: Tap water is excellent, soft Highland-sourced and safe everywhere.

transit.pay: The SPT Subway uses a contactless Bramble smartcard or paper tickets from station machines (a single is about £1.75, a day ticket around £4.40). Buses take contactless bank cards or exact cash on board with a First Bus daily fare cap, and ScotRail suburban trains are paid at station machines or via the app.
transit.hours: The Subway runs roughly 6:30am-11:30pm (Sundays about 10am-6:15pm); First Bus night services and ScotRail trains cover the wider city into the late evening.
transit.note: Glasgow's SPT Subway is a small 15-station loop (the 'Clockwork Orange') circling the city centre and West End; the dense ScotRail suburban rail network and First buses reach everywhere else.

transit.m: Glasgow Airport Express bus 500 to Buchanan Bus Station, ~15-25 min, up to every 10 min, 24/7
Local bus 77 to the city centre (cheaper, slower)

food.name: Haggis, neeps and tatties
food.desc: Spiced sheep's pluck with oatmeal, steamed and served with mashed turnip and potato, often with a whisky cream sauce.

places.name: Ubiquitous Chip
places.note: Ashton Lane institution since 1971 and a benchmark for modern Scottish cooking.

places.name: Stravaigin
places.note: Gibson Street favourite whose haggis is a long-standing menu fixture.

places.name: Glaschu
places.note: Contemporary Scottish dining room behind the Gallery of Modern Art.

food.name: Haggis pakora
food.desc: A Glasgow invention: haggis crumbled into gram-flour batter, deep fried and served with tamarind or spiced yoghurt.

places.name: Mother India's Cafe
places.note: Tapas-style Indian small plates on Argyle Street; the haggis pakora is a signature.

places.name: Babu Bombay Street Kitchen
places.note: Bright cafe doing Indian-Scottish street food and big breakfast plates.

places.name: The Wee Curry Shop
places.note: Tiny, long-running BYOB kitchen with a short, sharp menu.

food.name: Chicken tikka masala
food.desc: Tandoori chicken in a mild spiced tomato-and-cream gravy, a dish Glasgow claims to have invented in the 1970s.

places.name: Shish Mahal

places.name: Mother India

places.name: Koolba

food.desc: A slab of Lorne sausage griddled and folded into a buttered morning roll; Glasgow's default breakfast, often with tattie scone.

places.name: Cafe Gandolfi
places.note: Merchant City stalwart since 1979 with Scottish breakfast staples.

places.name: Singl-end
places.note: Popular all-day brunch basement doing generous Scottish breakfasts.

places.name: Riverhill Coffee Bar
places.note: Small Gordon Street counter known for excellent rolls and coffee.

food.name: Tablet
food.desc: Crumbly, grainy Scottish sugar-and-condensed-milk confection, harder and more brittle than fudge; sold by the slab.

places.name: Mackintosh at the Willow
places.note: Restored Charles Rennie Mackintosh tearooms serving tablet with afternoon tea.

places.name: The Barras Market
places.note: Weekend market in the East End with traditional sweet stalls.

places.name: Peckham's
places.note: Long-established Glasgow deli chain stocking Scottish tablet and shortbread.

food.name: Cullen skink and Scottish seafood
food.desc: Smoked haddock, potato and onion soup from the Moray coast, plus west-coast oysters, langoustines and mussels landed the same day.

places.name: Crabshakk
places.note: Small, much-loved seafood bar that helped make Finnieston a food street.

places.name: Gamba
places.note: Basement fish restaurant open since 1998 and a fixture in Scottish guides.

places.name: The Fish People Cafe
places.note: Cafe attached to a working fishmonger beside Shields Road subway.

food.name: Scotch whisky
food.desc: Single malts from every Scottish region, poured by the dram; Glasgow's old bars keep hundreds of bottles behind the gantry.

places.name: The Pot Still
places.note: Hope Street bar with a famous wall of several hundred malts.

places.name: The Bon Accord
places.note: Real-ale and whisky pub with a huge, well-kept malt list.

places.name: The Ben Nevis
places.note: Cosy Argyle Street bar with folk music and a serious whisky selection.

food.name: Irn-Bru
food.desc: Scotland's bright orange soft drink, sweeter and more citrus-bitter than cola, and the traditional cure for the morning after.

places.name: University Cafe
places.note: Byres Road cafe run by the same family since 1918; Irn-Bru with fish and chips.

places.name: Cafe Gandolfi

places.name: The Barras Market

landmarks: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum
One of Scotland's most-visited museums, this red sandstone Victorian showpiece houses everything from a Salvador Dalí masterpiece to a Spitfire suspended from the ceiling.
Glasgow Cathedral
A rare surviving medieval Scottish cathedral, its soaring Gothic nave and atmospheric crypt make it one of the city's most photographed historic buildings.
Glasgow Necropolis
A dramatic Victorian hillside cemetery of ornate monuments overlooking the cathedral, offering some of the best panoramic photo views in the city.
Riverside Museum
Zaha Hadid's zigzag-roofed transport museum on the Clyde is a striking piece of contemporary architecture and home to the historic Tall Ship Glenlee.
University of Glasgow (Gilbert Scott Building)
The soaring Gothic Revival spire and quadrangles of this 19th-century building make it one of the most iconic academic silhouettes in Scotland.
George Square
The grand civic heart of Glasgow, ringed by statues and the ornate City Chambers, and the traditional stage for the city's festivals and gatherings.
Clyde Auditorium ("The Armadillo") & SEC
Its distinctive shell-like, armadillo-shaped silhouette on the riverbank has made it an instantly recognizable emblem of modern Glasgow.
Equestrian Statue of the Duke of Wellington (with traffic cone)
Glasgow's most beloved and photographed inside joke: this grand statue almost always sports a traffic cone on its head, a symbol of the city's irreverent humor.
Kibble Palace (Botanic Gardens)
A gleaming Victorian glasshouse of curved glass and iron in the Botanic Gardens, filled with exotic plants and classical statuary.
Clyde Arc ("Squinty Bridge")
This sleek, curved bridge across the River Clyde has become a modern architectural landmark and a favorite subject for night photography.

train.note: No international trains from Glasgow - for Eurostar you travel to London St Pancras first. Avanti West Coast reaches London Euston in about 4h30 from Glasgow Central, and the Caledonian Sleeper (https://www.sleeper.scot/) runs overnight to London every night except Saturdays. Queen Street station handles the Edinburgh shuttle and the scenic West Highland Line to Fort William and Mallaig; the two stations are a 10-minute walk apart.

bus.note: No direct international coaches - continental services leave from London. Buchanan Bus Station is the Scottish hub, with Scottish Citylink (https://www.citylink.co.uk/) running to Edinburgh, Fort William, Skye and Inverness, and National Express and Megabus covering England. The Edinburgh coach is cheaper but slower than the train.

intl.to: Dunoon & Rothesay (UK) - sails from Gourock and Wemyss Bay, ~30-45 min by train from Glasgow
Arran, Islay, Mull & the Hebrides (UK) - sails from Ardrossan, Kennacraig and Oban

ferry.note: Nothing sails from Glasgow itself - the Clyde ferry ports are down the coast at Gourock, Wemyss Bay and Ardrossan, all reachable by direct ScotRail trains from the city in 30 to 60 minutes, with the train timed to meet the boat. CalMac serves the whole west coast island network; book vehicles well ahead in summer and expect weather cancellations. There are no international sailings from the Clyde.

half.name: Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park
half.blurb: Scotland's largest loch, ringed by hills and forest trails, reachable by train or coach in under an hour.

half.name: Stirling Castle
half.blurb: Renaissance royal castle on a volcanic crag overlooking the site of the Battle of Bannockburn.

half.name: Isle of Bute (Rothesay)
half.blurb: Ferry-linked island town with a Victorian promenade and a moated medieval castle at its center.

half.name: Inveraray
half.blurb: Loch Fyne town built around Inveraray Castle, ancestral seat of the Duke of Argyll, with a preserved 18th-century jail.

half.name: Edinburgh
half.blurb: Scotland's capital, with its castle, Royal Mile, and Georgian New Town, reachable by direct train in under an hour.
